By the authors' own numbers SORB delivers no accuracy benefit (test-orbit neutral; train-aug significantly worse, p=5e-8) while costing up to 6x inference and 4x training data, and its sole benefit — reduced per-prediction orbit spread — is obtainable at 1x cost by the obvious alternative the paper never tests: applying the training canonicalization (including tautomer canonicalization) to inference inputs. The computational analysis is also under-reported and partly inconsistent with the actual runs: SORB was evaluated only on 49/55 datasets (the 6 largest excluded for memory, never disclosed), timing claims are unmeasured, and core-count/runtime figures do not match the authoritative run. A practitioner reading this would reasonably choose "canonicalize consistently" over SORB.

findings.area: Deployment / missing baseline: the cheap alternative that defeats the method
findings.issue: The central deployment case for SORB-testorbit is that it makes a prediction '(nearly) independent of the arbitrary standardization of its input' (Sec 7.1). But the obvious, free alternative is never tested: apply the SAME canonicalization used at training (P_rdkit + canonical tautomer) to every inference input. In src/training/invariance.py the 'baseline' config feeds each test molecule's orbit members AS-IS (run_method_cell never re-canonicalizes test inputs), so its measured orbit SD is an artifact of NOT canonicalizing. A deployed model that canonicalizes its inputs maps every orbit member to one form (see canonical_identity() in standardize.py, which collapses tautomer/charge/salt/stereo to a single key) and is therefore EXACTLY invariant at 1x cost, versus SORB's only-approximate invariance at up to 6x inference cost with no accuracy gain. For cross-lab agreement SORB still requires a shared orbit definition and averaging convention, so it does not remove the coordination requirement — it makes the required convention ~6x more expensive. Without this comparison the reader cannot judge whether SORB is ever worth adopting.
findings.evidence: manuscript Sec 7.1 (line 298-301) 'free reliability improvement'; invariance.py run_method_cell uses Xcanon only for baseline/trainaug accuracy and measures baseline invariance via _pipeline_matrix/_orbit_invariance on un-recanonicalized members; metrics.json RQ4 shows testorbit accuracy median improvement -7.45e-5 (p=0.8), i.e. no accuracy upside to offset the 6x cost; canonical_identity() proves a 1x canonical collapse exists.
findings.fix: Add a 'canonicalize-at-inference' baseline (apply the full training standardization, including canonical tautomer, to every test input) and report its orbit SD (should be ~0) and accuracy against SORB-testorbit. If canonicalize-at-inference matches SORB on reliability at 1x cost, reframe SORB's niche to the specific case where input standardization cannot be controlled or the canonical form is tool-ambiguous, and state this explicitly in Discussion/Sec 9.

findings.area: Honest overhead reporting: 'free' conflates no-accuracy-cost with no-compute-cost
findings.issue: Sec 7.1 calls test-time orbit averaging 'a free reliability improvement' and Sec 9 calls it 'the cost-effective default', yet Sec 9 itself states it 'multiplies inference cost by the orbit size (at most 6)'. 'Free' is accurate only for accuracy, not for compute: 6x inference latency, throughput, and energy are first-order deployment concerns (batch scoring of large libraries, latency-bound services). No inference-latency, throughput, or energy numbers are given anywhere; there is no cost-benefit quantification backing 'cost-effective'.
findings.evidence: manuscript line 298 'free reliability improvement'; lines 344-348 Sec 9 admits '6x' inference but provides no measured latency/throughput; no cost column in any table (tables/table3_method.csv contains only accuracy/invariance).
findings.fix: Replace 'free' with 'accuracy-neutral at up to 6x inference cost'. Report measured inference latency/throughput for baseline vs SORB-testorbit on a representative dataset, and state when the 6x is and is not acceptable (e.g., single-compound decision support vs million-compound virtual screening).

findings.area: Scope non-disclosure: SORB untested on the largest datasets, where cost and the problem are worst
findings.issue: SORB (method + shortcut) ran only on the 49 datasets with <=6000 molecules; the 6 largest (up to cyp2d6_veith, 13,130 mol) were excluded because, per the run_all.py code comment, 'orbit augmentation on very large sets is memory-heavy'. The manuscript never states this: the strings '49' and '6000' do not appear in manuscript_filled.md, and Sec 8 claims the method-level conclusions hold '(iv) across the 55 datasets'. The excluded CYP-inhibition sets are exactly the large, highly-ionizable/tautomerizable datasets where RQ3 predicts the invariance violation is worst AND where 6x inference cost hurts most — so the method's deployability is unvalidated precisely where it matters, and the overhead/scalability limitation is hidden.
findings.evidence: run_all.py lines 183-191 'cap to datasets <= METHOD_MAX_N ... memory-heavy', METHOD_MAX_N=6000; metrics.json RQ5b n_datasets=49; full_run5.log '[E4/E5 method ...] on 49/55 datasets (<= 6000 mol)'; table1_datasets.csv max N=13,130 with 6 datasets >6000; manuscript Sec 8 line 336 '(iv) across the 55 datasets'; grep shows no '49'/'6000' in manuscript.
findings.fix: State clearly that SORB was evaluated on 49/55 datasets (<=6000 molecules) and why (memory), and correct Sec 8 to not claim 55. Add this as an explicit Limitation. To actually support deployment claims, run SORB (at least test-orbit averaging, which has no training-memory issue) on the 6 large datasets, or demonstrate a streaming/memory-bounded augmentation implementation.

findings.area: Unsupported timing claim for orbit construction
findings.issue: Sec 9 states 'building orbits for the largest dataset (13,130 molecules) takes under a minute on one core.' There is no timing instrumentation that isolates orbit construction anywhere in src/ (grep for perf_counter/time in src returns nothing; the only time.time() calls in run_all.py report cumulative per-20-job wall time mixed with featurization, inside a parallel Pool, not single-core orbit-only time). The authoritative run that produced metrics.json (full_run5.log) skipped precompute entirely (no '[precompute caches]' line), so no orbit was built in that run, and the 13,130-molecule dataset's orbit is never even used by SORB (it is one of the 6 excluded). The claim is an unverified assertion about a cost the method never actually pays.
findings.evidence: manuscript lines 343-345; grep 'perf_counter|elapsed|timeit' in src/ returns nothing; cache.py dataset_orbits has no timing; full_run5.log begins at '[E1/E2 sensitivity grid]' with no precompute stage; dataset excluded per METHOD_MAX_N=6000.
findings.fix: Either measure orbit-construction time explicitly (single core, isolated, reported with RDKit/Dimorphite-DL versions) on representative datasets and report the number with its provenance, or remove the specific claim. Do not cite the 13,130-molecule dataset's orbit time when that orbit is not used by the method.

findings.area: Runtime/hardware figures inconsistent with the actual authoritative run
findings.issue: Sec 9 says 'All experiments run on four CPU cores ... the complete study completes in a few hours.' The authoritative run that wrote metrics.json (full_run5.log, timestamped with metrics.json) used nproc=2, and results were in fact accreted across five separate cached runs using 1, 2, 3, and 4 cores. Because caching makes every sensitivity/ablation/method step report '(0s)' in that run, no single cold end-to-end timing of 'a few hours' was ever actually produced; it is an estimate (run_all.py docstring says '~2 h on 4 cores') presented as a measured fact.
findings.evidence: grep of logs: full_run.log nproc=4, full_run2 nproc=2, full_run3 nproc=3, full_run4 nproc=1, full_run5 nproc=2; full_run5.log shows every sens/abl/method step '(0s)' (cached), only shortcut takes 558s; run_all.py line 157 default nproc and docstring '~2 h wall on 4 cores'.
findings.fix: Report the actual hardware/core count used for the authoritative run and give a measured cold (cache-cleared) end-to-end wall time, or clearly label the runtime as an estimate. Reconcile '4 cores' with the 2-core authoritative run.

findings.area: Cost-benefit of train-time augmentation not honestly weighed
findings.issue: Train-aug costs 4x training data (train_aug=4 in run_method_cell / SORB) yet significantly WORSENS regression accuracy (pooled median improvement -0.013 RMSE, only 32% of cases improved, Wilcoxon p=5.1e-8; for linear+ECFP regression mean -3.29 RMSE, catastrophic). Its only benefit is a 36% reduction in orbit SD — which, as in Finding 1, is obtainable at 1x via consistent canonicalization. The paper recommends train-aug 'specifically for robust (tree-ensemble) learners' where it is ~neutral, but neutral accuracy at 4x training cost with a reliability gain that a free alternative already provides is not a deployment win, and this trade is never framed as a cost-benefit decision.
findings.evidence: metrics.json RQ4 reg_sorb_trainaug median -0.013, frac 0.319, p=5.14e-08; statistics.json linear/ecfp/reg trainaug mean_improvement -3.29 RMSE; trainaug_invariance 36.3% reduction; SORB default train_aug=4 (sorb.py line 35, invariance.py line 70).
findings.fix: Present train-aug as a cost (4x data) vs benefit (invariance reduction only, no accuracy gain, possible accuracy loss) decision, and justify the 'adopt for trees' recommendation against the free canonicalize-at-inference alternative rather than only against the as-is baseline.

findings.area: 'Accuracy-neutral' claim rests on mismatched test sets
findings.issue: The headline that test-orbit averaging is 'accuracy-neutral' (justifying its cost by reliability alone) compares baseline accuracy computed on the FULL test set against SORB-testorbit/full accuracy computed on a <=600-molecule random subsample (ACC_CAP=600). For the 6 method datasets with n_test>600 (max 840) the paired comparison is on different test subsets, confounding the very 'no accuracy cost' conclusion that the compute justification depends on.
findings.evidence: invariance.py lines 24, 80-81, 97, 104-108: baseline uses predict_scores(..., Xcanon[te]) on full te; sorb_testorbit/sorb_full use est.predict(cap_smi, ...) with cap capped at ACC_CAP=600; method_results.csv: 6/49 datasets have n_test>600 (max 840).
findings.fix: Compute all variants' accuracy on the identical (capped) test subset, or raise/remove the cap, and re-report the testorbit accuracy-neutrality (Wilcoxon over datasets) on matched samples.

summary: The analysis pipeline is genuinely reproducible: analyze.py regenerates results/metrics.json and results/statistics.json bit-for-bit from the committed raw CSVs, tables regenerate identically (git tree stays clean), figures/tables read only from machine-readable result files (no hand-entered numbers), 11 unit tests pass, seeds are set and runs are checkpointed/resumable, and the headline numbers (0.51% aggregate spread, 0.10x orbit SD, 0.032/36%/91% train-aug reduction, -0.0001 test-orbit p=0.8, 0.102 shortcut drop p=5e-10, invariance table 0.084/0.119/0.071/0.425, leakage 82/2832/851) all trace correctly to the result files. However, the manuscript, README, and requirements describe a protocol and environment that were not actually executed: it claims four model families (incl. a Nystrom SVM that was dropped) and five seeds, when the code and committed data used three models and three seeds; the pinned package versions do not match the versions that produced the results; and two results are mis-reported (Section 6.4 contradicts its own table; the shortcut headline pools non-commensurable units). These are fixable, mostly by correcting text to match the executed run, but they currently make the paper non-reproducible as described and internally contradictory.

findings.area: Protocol vs. executed run (manuscript/README contradict code and data)
findings.issue: The manuscript Section 5 states 'four model families: gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM), random forests, an RBF-kernel SVM via Nystrom approximation, and a linear model' and 'Each configuration is run with five seeds'; README says 'the full study uses seeds 0-4'. The code and committed results used only THREE models and THREE seeds. src/training/grid.py: MODELS = ['lgbm','rf','linear']  # svm(Nystroem) dropped: costly, least informative; full-mode seeds=[0,1,2], method_seeds=[0,1,2], shortcut_seeds=[0,1,2]. results/experiment_logs/run_meta_full.json and raw_results.csv confirm models={lgbm,linear,rf}, seeds={0,1,2}; RQ1 n_cells=330 = 55 datasets x 3 models x 2 feats (no SVM). The SVM is described in detail and unit-tested but never appears in any result. The abstract and contributions say '3 model families', directly contradicting Section 5's 'four'. This is also an undisclosed deviation from the pre-registration (research_plan.md: '5 model families', 'R = 5 scaffold resplits (seeds 0-4)', 'R = 10 for the headline SORB and RQ2'); the 2026-11-16 amendment reframes the headline but does not document the model/seed reduction.
findings.evidence: A reader cannot reproduce 'four model families, five seeds' from the repo; run_all.py only produces three models and three seeds. The manuscript's stated methods thus do not match the released code or the numbers in metrics.json, and the abstract/Section 5 disagree on the model count.
findings.fix: Correct Section 5 to 'three model families' (LightGBM, random forest, linear) and 'three seeds (0-2)'; remove the Nystrom-SVM description or explicitly state it was implemented but dropped from the reported grid; fix README 'seeds 0-4' -> 'seeds 0-2' and the layout note that lists Nystroem-SVM; and add a 'deviations from pre-registration' note. Alternatively, to honor the pre-registration, actually run the 5-seed/4-model grid (new experiment). The text-only correction requires no new experiment.

findings.area: Environment pinning (requirements.txt / environment.yml do not match run environment)
findings.issue: requirements.txt is commented 'Versions pinned to what the study was run with' and pins numpy==2.5.3 and scipy==1.18.1, but the environment that actually produced the results has numpy 2.3.5 and scipy 1.17.1 (verified via importlib.metadata in the container). numpy 2.5.3 does not appear to exist in this environment's package set (the installed 2.x line tops out at 2.3.5), so `pip install -r requirements.txt` would either fail to resolve or install a different version than was used, breaking the determinism claim. environment.yml repeats the mismatched numpy=2.5/scipy=1.18 pins.
findings.evidence: Pinned numpy==2.5.3/scipy==1.18.1 vs. actually-used numpy 2.3.5/scipy 1.17.1. A third party following the README cannot recreate the exact environment, undermining 'Determinism: fixed seeds; results cached' and 'environment specifications ... released'.
findings.fix: Regenerate requirements.txt and environment.yml from an exact `pip freeze` / `conda env export` of the machine that produced results/*.csv, verify every pin installs cleanly from a clean venv, and (if feasible) confirm run_all.py --mode quick + analyze reproduce the cached cells under those pins.

findings.area: Results reporting: Section 6.4 contradicts its own Table (tbl:inv)
findings.issue: Section 6.4 states the orbit SD 'is smallest for gradient-boosted trees on fingerprints (0.12x of the label SD) and largest for linear models on fingerprints (0.42x...)'. The paper's own Table tbl:inv (and metrics.json RQ5_invariance) show lgbm/desc=0.084 and linear/desc=0.071, both SMALLER than lgbm/ecfp=0.119. So 0.12x is not the smallest value; the minimum is linear-on-descriptors (0.071).
findings.evidence: The sentence mis-ranks the four cells against the adjacent table, which a careful reviewer/reader will catch as an internal inconsistency and which weakens the 'representation-dependent' narrative.
findings.fix: Reword to e.g. 'smallest for descriptor-based models (~0.07-0.08x) and, among fingerprint models, smallest for gradient-boosted trees (0.12x) and largest for linear models (0.42x)'.

findings.area: Code/statistics correctness: shortcut headline pools non-commensurable units
findings.issue: Section 7.3's headline 'accuracy ... dropping by 0.102 in the primary metric (median over datasets)' is computed in analyze.rq5b_shortcut as pooled.baseline_shortcut_drop.median() over all 49 datasets, i.e. a single median taken across 40 regression RMSE drops AND 9 classification AUROC drops. src/training/shortcut.py computes baseline_shortcut_drop as a raw RMSE difference for regression (not normalized by label SD, unlike the invariance analysis which uses *_rel_sd) and an AUROC difference for classification. Per-task the drops are reg median 0.1128 (RMSE, in each dataset's own label units, unnormalized across datasets with very different label scales) vs clf median 0.0342 (AUROC); the pooled 0.102 is dominated by, and mostly inherits the arbitrary scale of, the regression RMSE values.
findings.evidence: A median over mixed RMSE-and-AUROC quantities (and over RMSE values on datasets with incomparable label ranges) is not an interpretable single effect size; '0.102 in the primary metric' conflates units. Contrast the invariance metric, which the authors correctly normalize by label SD.
findings.fix: Report the shortcut drop separately for regression and classification, and normalize the regression drop by each dataset's label SD (a dimensionless relative drop) before taking any median, mirroring the orbit_mean_rel_sd convention. The label SDs are available from the dataset loaders, so this is a re-analysis of existing shortcut_results.csv, not a new experiment.

reviewer: Associate Editor — writing, structure, figures/tables, references, JCIM scope & author-guideline compliance
summary: The core study is in-scope for JCIM, clearly motivated, and the honest-reporting framing (invariance violation hidden by aggregate metrics; SORB as a reliability not accuracy method) is a genuine strength. However, as an editorial package the submission is incomplete and would not clear screening: the Supporting Information is an unpopulated template (literal {{N_DATASETS}} tokens, no actual Tables S1-S4 or Figures S1-S4) even though the main text leans on it for the leakage audit, full results, ablation, and robustness; and the main-text table apparatus is broken (a referenced "Table 3" is absent, the only embedded table is never cited, Table 1 is missing). Several claims also over-reach or contradict the paper's own numbers (abstract "benefits tree-based learners," "smallest for GBT on fingerprints," an undisclosed 49/55-dataset restriction, a model family with no reported results, inconsistent seed counts). None of the fixes require new experiments except, optionally, reporting the already-named SVM model.

findings.area: Supporting Information / editorial screening
findings.issue: The Supporting Information (Target_Journal_Submission/supplementary/supplementary.md) is a 39-line unpopulated skeleton: it contains a literal unresolved placeholder ({{N_DATASETS}}) and only prose descriptions of what Tables S1-S4 and Figures S1-S4 'will' contain — no actual tables, numbers, or figures. findings.area: Abstract / overclaiming vs. data

Its only non-negative effects for lgbm are on classification and are non-significant.

findings.fix: Reframe train-aug's benefit strictly as invariance reduction, and state plainly that it carries a small but statistically significant accuracy cost even for tree learners on regression. Change the abstract wording from 'benefits robust (tree-based) learners' accordingly.

summary: The core thesis — "aggregate metrics robust, per-prediction not, therefore use SORB" — survives the shallow "it's just ensemble averaging" objection (the per-prediction orbit SD is genuine model sensitivity to different fingerprints, not an averaging artifact). But the paper collapses under a deeper attack: the entire "violation" is manufactured by comparing against a strawman baseline (P_rdkit) that deliberately omits tautomer canonicalization — the very operation RQ3 identifies as dominant — while the authors already implement deterministic canonical-tautomer standardization in canonical_identity() and use it for deduplication. A canonical-tautomer-once pipeline collapses the orbit to a single point, yielding EXACT invariance at 1x inference cost, dominating SORB-testorbit (approximate invariance, 6x cost) on every axis; this essential baseline is never run, so the paper's claim that invariance requires SORB is unsupported, and the work reduces to "preprocessing matters, use a consistent canonical pipeline." Compounding this are verifiable integrity defects: the manuscript claims "five seeds" and "four model families including an RBF-kernel SVM," but every result file contains only three seeds (0,1,2) and three models (lgbm/linear/rf) with no SVM anywhere; the testorbit reliability benefit is asserted but never measured; and the "benefits tree learners / accuracy-neutral" claim is contradicted by the authors' own significance tests.

findings.area: Core contribution / Method necessity (Sec 4, 6.4, 7.1)
findings.issue: The central claim that standardization-invariance 'requires' SORB is established only against a baseline (P_rdkit = largest-fragment + neutralize) that OMITS tautomer canonicalization, which RQ3 (metrics.json RQ3_ablation: +tautomer is the only non-zero operation, 0.006) identifies as the dominant driver of the orbit spread. The authors already implement a deterministic canonical-tautomer standardizer (standardize.py op_canonical_tautomer, used in canonical_identity() for dedup), which collapses the orbit's tautomer axis to a single point. A 'canonical-tautomer-once' pipeline (applied identically to train and test) therefore yields EXACT invariance to input presentation at 1x inference cost with no new convention, strictly dominating SORB-testorbit (approximate, order-truncated, 6x cost). This obvious, cheaper, exactly-invariant baseline is never evaluated, so the paper's core premise ('the silent confounder requires a remedy') and the recommendation of test-time orbit averaging as 'the safe universal default' are unsupported. The work reduces to the known advice 'use a consistent canonical pipeline.'
findings.evidence: run_method_cell (invariance.py L78,96): baseline trained on features(...,'P_rdkit',...), i.e. no tautomer canonicalization. NAMED_PIPELINES['P_rdkit'] has canonical_tautomer=False (standardize.py L179). canonical_identity() (L200-214) DOES apply op_canonical_tautomer, proving the authors have an orbit-collapsing canonicalizer in hand but chose a baseline that omits it. RQ3 shows tautomer is the sole material operation. No experiment trains+tests a canonical-tautomer model and measures its residual orbit SD (which would be ~0 on the dominant axis).
findings.fix: Add a canonical-tautomer-once baseline (P_taut-style: fix tautomer + one protonation + one aromaticity model, applied to train and test) and report its per-prediction orbit SD and accuracy against SORB-testorbit. SORB can only be a contribution if it beats this baseline on reliability-at-equal-cost or on accuracy; otherwise reframe the paper as a reporting-protocol/diagnosis paper and drop the SORB-necessity claims.
findings.short_summary: No canonical-tautomer baseline; it would give exact invariance at 1x cost
findings.failure_scenario: A reviewer/competitor runs canonical-tautomer-once standardization on train+test: orbit SD on the dominant tautomer axis -> ~0 at 1x inference cost, matching or beating SORB-testorbit's approximate invariance at 6x cost, nullifying the method's reason to exist.

findings.area: Experimental Setup (Sec 5, L185-187) vs result files
findings.issue: Section 5 states the study uses 'four model families: gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM), random forests, an RBF-kernel SVM via Nyström approximation, and a linear model.' No SVM appears in ANY result file (raw_results/ablation/method/shortcut models = {lgbm, linear, rf} only). The pre-registration also listed SVM and a tiny MLP consistency variant. Separately, the Abstract/Contributions/Conclusion say '3 model families,' internally contradicting Section 5's 'four.' This is a methodology claim (an RBF-kernel SVM) for which no evidence exists in the released results.
findings.evidence: grep of manuscript L19/71/381 ('3 model families') vs L185-186 ('four model families ... RBF-kernel SVM via Nystrom'). CSV scan: raw_results/ablation_results models={lgbm,linear,rf}; method_results/shortcut_results models={lgbm,linear}. 'SVM'/'Nystrom' appears nowhere in results. MLP consistency variant (claimed in Sec 4.2/SI) likewise absent.
findings.fix: Either run the SVM (and MLP) and include results, or delete every claim of an SVM/MLP model family and reconcile the model-family count throughout (it is 3: lgbm, linear, rf). State explicitly which models were actually run for each RQ.
findings.short_summary: Claimed RBF-SVM model family absent from all results; 3-vs-4 count conflict
findings.failure_scenario: An editor checks the repo for the SVM results promised in Section 5, finds none, and concludes the methods section describes experiments that were not performed.

findings.area: Statistics / reproducibility (Sec 5, L211)
findings.issue: Section 5 states 'Each configuration is run with five seeds,' and the pre-registration specified R=5 for the grid and R=10 for the headline SORB/RQ2 comparisons. Every result file contains only seeds {0,1,2} = three seeds. The SORB section (L294) quietly says 'three seeds' while Section 5 says 'five' — an internal contradiction and an undisclosed, unexplained deviation from both the stated methods and the pre-registration that reduces statistical power on the headline null results.
findings.evidence: CSV seed scan: raw_results/method_results/shortcut_results/ablation_results all = {'0','1','2'}. Manuscript L211 'five seeds' vs L294 'three seeds'. research_plan.md L120-121: 'R = 5 scaffold resplits ... R = 10 for the headline SORB and RQ2 comparisons.' The pre-registration amendment does not mention reducing seeds.
findings.fix: Correct Section 5 to the true seed count, run the pre-registered seed counts (5 grid / 10 headline) or explicitly justify the reduction as a disclosed deviation, and re-derive all p-values/CIs. Note that under-seeding directly weakens the non-significant 'accuracy-neutral' claims (see next finding).
findings.short_summary: 'Five seeds' claimed and R=10 pre-registered, but only 3 seeds were run
findings.failure_scenario: A replicator following the pre-registration runs 5/10 seeds, obtains different CIs/p-values, and the 'accuracy-neutral' null (currently p=0.8 at 3 seeds) changes, because the paper's power was overstated.

findings.area: SORB error analysis (Sec 7.1-7.2, L300-318)
findings.issue: The paper claims training augmentation 'benefits robust (tree-based) learners' and that 'for the gradient-boosted-tree learner it is roughly accuracy-neutral.' The authors' own per-cell statistics show lgbm training augmentation SIGNIFICANTLY WORSENS regression RMSE on both featurizations: lgbm/ecfp/reg median -0.0148, p=5.8e-6, improved on only 22.5% of datasets; lgbm/desc/reg median -0.0101, p=0.02, improved on 35%. Pooled regression trainaug is significantly worse (metrics.json reg_sorb_trainaug median -0.013, p=5.1e-8, 32% improved). Trainaug is positive only on classification and only non-significantly. The 'benefits tree learners / accuracy-neutral for GBDT' framing is directly contradicted by the significance tests.
findings.evidence: statistics.json: lgbm/ecfp/reg/sorb_trainaug median_improvement -0.01483, wilcoxon_p 5.8e-6, frac_improved 0.225; lgbm/desc/reg/sorb_trainaug median -0.01006, p=0.0200, frac 0.35. metrics.json RQ4_method_pooled.reg_sorb_trainaug: median -0.013, p=5.1e-8, frac_improved 0.319.
findings.fix: Rewrite Sec 7.1-7.2 to state that trainaug significantly degrades tree-learner regression accuracy (not neutral), and restrict any accuracy-positive claim to the specific (classification, non-significant) cells. Do not describe a significantly-worse result (p=5.8e-6) as 'roughly accuracy-neutral.'
findings.short_summary: Trainaug significantly worsens lgbm RMSE, not 'accuracy-neutral' as claimed
findings.failure_scenario: A reader cross-references Table 3 / statistics.json and finds the GBDT trainaug RMSE change is significantly negative (p=5.8e-6), directly contradicting the sentence calling it 'roughly accuracy-neutral.'

findings.area: Test-orbit 'free reliability' claim (Sec 7.1, L298-300)
findings.issue: 'Accuracy-neutral,' 'no significant accuracy cost,' and 'a free reliability improvement' are all inferred from NON-significant Wilcoxon tests (reg testorbit p=0.8, clf p=0.90). Failing to reject the null is not evidence of equivalence; no equivalence test (e.g., TOST) or negligibility margin is specified. The per-cell CIs are wide and include non-negligible accuracy harm: lgbm/ecfp/reg/testorbit RMSE-change CI = [-0.0077, +0.1446] and lgbm/desc/reg/testorbit CI upper = +0.1029 — i.e., up to ~0.14 RMSE degradation is consistent with the data. 'Accuracy-neutral' is therefore unestablished.
findings.evidence: statistics.json: lgbm/ecfp/reg/sorb_testorbit ci_lo -0.0077, ci_hi 0.1446; lgbm/desc/reg/sorb_testorbit ci_hi 0.1029; linear/ecfp/reg/sorb_testorbit mean +0.315, ci_hi 0.629. metrics.json reg_sorb_testorbit p=0.805. Manuscript L298-300 asserts neutrality from p=0.8.
findings.fix: Replace null-acceptance language with a formal equivalence test against a pre-stated negligibility margin (e.g., fraction of label SD), and report that for several model/featurization cells the CI admits meaningful accuracy loss. More seeds (see seed finding) will tighten these CIs.
findings.short_summary: 'Accuracy-neutral' claimed from p>0.05 with CIs admitting +0.14 RMSE harm
findings.failure_scenario: A statistician notes the testorbit RMSE CI reaches +0.14 and that no equivalence test was run, so 'free reliability improvement' is an unjustified acceptance of the null.

findings.area: Test-orbit 'enforces invariance' (Abstract; Sec 4.2; Sec 7.1)
findings.issue: The reliability benefit of SORB-testorbit — the paper's recommended universal default — is asserted 'by construction' but never measured: in run_method_cell the invariance metrics (_pipeline_matrix/_orbit_invariance) are computed only for the baseline and trainaug rows; for sorb_testorbit and sorb_full, base_row is called with inv_model=None, so no orbit SD is recorded for the averaged predictor. Worse, the construction does not actually guarantee the claimed invariance 'to which member was presented': standardization_orbit() is seeded by the presented SMILES (member[0] = P_rdkit(smiles), which does NOT canonicalize tautomers), and the member list is truncated to max_members in insertion order, so two chemically-equivalent input tautomers generate different (order-truncated) orbits and therefore different averages. The abstract's 'makes the output independent of which member was presented' is false as implemented (true only in the unrealized 'complete orbit' limit).
findings.evidence: invariance.py L104-108: for ('sorb_testorbit', base) and ('sorb_full', ...), base_row(method, _acc(...), None) -> inv_model=None, so orbit SD never computed for averaged variants. standardize.py L233 base=P_rdkit.apply(smiles) (no canonical_tautomer), L269 members[:cfg.max_members] (order-dependent truncation). No experiment presents the same molecule as different input forms and checks that the testorbit average is invariant.
findings.fix: Directly measure cross-presentation invariance of SORB-testorbit: for each test molecule, generate the orbit from several different starting members, average each, and report the residual SD of the averaged prediction (should be ~0 if the claim holds). Fix the orbit construction to be canonicalization-seeded (start from the canonical-tautomer identity, not P_rdkit) so the orbit is genuinely input-independent, or soften the 'enforces invariance' claim to 'reduces, but does not eliminate, presentation dependence.'
findings.short_summary: Testorbit invariance never measured; input-seeded orbit is not presentation-invariant
findings.failure_scenario: Feeding the same molecule as two valid tautomers produces two different order-truncated orbits and two different averaged predictions, falsifying 'independent of which member was presented,' and the paper has no measurement to the contrary.

findings.area: Headline effect size (Abstract; Sec 6.4)
findings.issue: The alarming headline figure (orbit SD up to 0.42x label SD) is for linear-on-ECFP — a high-variance model essentially nobody deploys for production QSAR, which the paper itself calls the most unstable learner. For the recommended/most-used model (LightGBM) the orbit SD is 0.084x (desc) to 0.119x (ecfp) of the label SD, which the paper concedes is 'comparable to a fraction of experimental assay noise' (~0.3-0.5 log units for potency). The 'material irreproducibility' narrative is driven by a strawman worst case; for the models practitioners actually use, the effect is at or below assay noise, undercutting the urgency.
findings.evidence: metrics.json RQ5_invariance: lgbm/desc 0.0843, lgbm/ecfp 0.1191, linear/desc 0.0715, linear/ecfp 0.4247. Manuscript L257-265 concedes 'comparable to a fraction of experimental assay noise.' The 0.42x worst case is linear/ecfp only.
findings.fix: Lead with the effect for deployed models (trees), state explicitly that the 0.42x case is a high-variance linear model not used in practice, and quantify the orbit SD against measured assay reproducibility per endpoint so readers can judge materiality. Temper 'material irreproducibility' accordingly.
findings.short_summary: Headline 0.42x is a non-deployed model; deployed-model effect is below assay noise
findings.failure_scenario: A practitioner using LightGBM sees orbit SD ~0.1x label SD < assay noise and concludes the reported problem does not materially affect real pipelines, i.e., the motivation is inflated.

findings.area: Semi-synthetic shortcut experiment (Sec 7.3; shortcut.py)
findings.issue: The 'controlled validation' is near-tautological: the standardization shortcut is INJECTED by construction (shortcut.py _present() picks orbit member by the true label), so a model that averages over the orbit (destroying the injected correlation) cannot exploit it 'by construction' — SORB wins because the experiment is built so it must. It provides no evidence that naturally-occurring standardization leaks into real labels. Moreover the framing 'accuracy collapses when the shortcut is removed' overstates: the counterfactual baseline is only 0.016 worse than the honest model (median baseline_cf_vs_honest=0.016), i.e., removing the injected leak returns the model to ~honest performance; the 0.102 'drop' is measured against the artificially inflated biased number, not against honest accuracy.
findings.evidence: shortcut.py L33-42 _present() selects member by hi_mask (true label). metrics.json RQ5b: median_baseline_shortcut_drop 0.1022 (biased->cf) but median_baseline_cf_vs_honest only 0.0164 (cf vs honest). So counterfactual accuracy ~ honest; the 'collapse' is loss of inflated accuracy, not degradation below honest.
findings.fix: Either (a) demonstrate NATURAL standardization-label leakage in real benchmarks (e.g., whether provider standardization state correlates with labels), which would be a genuine finding, or (b) downgrade Sec 7.3 to an illustrative sanity check and remove 'confirms that standard models exploit standardization as a shortcut,' clarifying that the shortcut is injected and that counterfactual accuracy returns to honest baseline.
findings.short_summary: Shortcut is injected so SORB resists by construction; 'collapse' is only vs inflated number
findings.failure_scenario: A reviewer notes the counterfactual model is only 0.016 worse than honest, so nothing 'collapses'; the experiment merely shows injected leakage helps when present and is removed when you destroy it — a tautology, not evidence of real-world shortcut exploitation.

findings.area: Robustness/Generalization (Sec 8, L336; Sec 7)
findings.issue: SORB and the shortcut experiments ran on 49 datasets (<=6000 molecules) and only 2 models (lgbm, linear), but Section 8 claims the findings are consistent '(iv) across the 55 datasets,' and the headline invariance table (Tbl inv) reports only lgbm and linear, omitting random forests (the other 'tree ensemble') despite the paper's repeated 'tree ensembles are least sensitive' messaging resting on trees. The method-section 'across datasets' statements never disclose n=49 or the 2-model restriction.
findings.evidence: method_results/shortcut_results: n_datasets=49, models={lgbm,linear}. Manuscript L336 'across the 55 datasets' (SORB). RQ5_invariance table (metrics.json) has only lgbm/linear x desc/ecfp; rf absent though raw_results includes rf. Sec 7.1 'across datasets (three seeds)' gives no n.
findings.fix: State the SORB/shortcut evaluation scope explicitly (49 datasets <=6000 mols; models lgbm and linear only), correct 'across the 55 datasets' in Sec 8, and either add RF to the SORB/invariance evaluation or stop citing RF robustness in method claims.
findings.short_summary: SORB ran on 49 datasets / 2 models but text says '55 datasets'; RF omitted
findings.failure_scenario: A reader counts datasets in the released SORB results (49), finds no RF and no SVM, and the Section 8 generalization claim ('across the 55 datasets') is demonstrably false.

findings.area: The 'silent confounder' framing (Sec 6.2 vs 6.4)
findings.issue: The rhetorical contrast 'aggregate robust, per-prediction not' compares two quantities that cannot reflect each other by construction: the aggregate metric is computed with every molecule in ONE internally-consistent pipeline (so per-molecule shifts cancel across the test set), while the orbit SD deliberately varies each molecule across its orbit. The aggregate metric is 'blind' to orbit variance tautologically, because orbit members are never fed into the aggregate. The scenario that would actually move the aggregate — each test molecule presented as an independently/randomly drawn orbit member (a lab that standardizes inconsistently per-compound) — is not directly tested; the reported pipeline SD (0.004-0.029 relative) stays tiny only because each pipeline is internally consistent, so it does not probe the per-molecule-random case.
findings.evidence: invariance.py _pipeline_matrix presents whole-dataset pipelines (consistent per pipeline); _inv_stats/_orbit_invariance present per-molecule orbits. No configuration evaluates aggregate accuracy under per-molecule random orbit draws. metrics.json RQ1 pipe SD 0.004-0.0286 (consistent pipelines) vs orbit SD 0.07-0.42.
findings.fix: Add an aggregate-under-random-per-molecule-standardization experiment to show whether/when inconsistent per-compound standardization degrades aggregate metrics; otherwise temper the 'aggregate metrics hide it' claim to acknowledge it is a definitional consequence of measuring aggregate under one consistent pipeline.
findings.short_summary: Aggregate vs orbit-SD contrast compares non-comparable quantities; key case untested
findings.failure_scenario: A critic points out that aggregate metrics cannot reflect orbit variance when orbit members are never presented in aggregate evaluation, so 'the aggregate hides it' is true by definition, not a discovered confounder.

findings.area: Abstract/Table consistency
findings.issue: Model-family count is stated as both '3' (Abstract L19, Contributions L71, Conclusion L381) and 'four' (Sec 5 L185); and headline invariance numbers appear as '0.10x median' (text) vs table values that round differently (0.084-0.119 for trees, 0.425 for linear/ecfp). The abstract's '3 model families' happens to match the 3 models actually run, which further exposes the Section-5 'four (incl. SVM)' claim as spurious.
findings.evidence: Manuscript L19/71/381 '3 model families' vs L185 'four model families.' Table inv values 0.084/0.119/0.071/0.425 vs abstract 'up to 0.42x' and 'median 0.10x.'
findings.fix: Reconcile the model-family count to the true value (3: lgbm, linear, rf) throughout, and ensure every quoted statistic matches the result files exactly.
findings.short_summary: Model-family count stated as both 3 and 4 in the same paper
findings.failure_scenario: A copy-editor or reviewer flags the 3-vs-4 contradiction and, on checking, discovers the 'four' version includes a model (SVM) absent from all results.
